chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
title: Washington's five big bands: Baldwin, Pete Moss, Hester, Tommy Miles, Booker Coleman
summary: A tour of U Street clubs and bands, including Tommy Miles's Cotton Club band with Trummy Young, Jimmy Mundy and Tyree Glenn.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: During this time, what I learned was that this fellow, Mr. Satterwhite, that owned the place, would hire two musicians, and before the night was over, we would have anywhere from 8 to 10, and sometimes even 12 musicians up there playing, and it would be guys that would drop in from other places or other jobs that they had. At that time, Washington had five big bands, big local bands in it, and there were... One band, Bill Baldwin's Syncopators played at a place on the 1200 block of U Street called the Lincoln Colonnade.

Just two blocks down the street from there, at Tenth and U Street, was the Masonic Ballroom, where they featured two bands. One was called... A fellow named Pete Moss had a band, and there was another fellow who I think is still around, and his name was Bill Hester, and Bill Hester called his band The Bluebirds. They started alternating at the Masonic Ballroom, and about every two weeks they would bring in somebody like Earl Hines or Duke Ellington, Cab Calloway, one of the big

But right down under this building there was a nightclub where they had chorus girls and all of that, and they called it the Cotton Club. That was also at Tenth and U, and that featured... The band there was under the leadership of a drummer, a fellow named Tommy Miles. That was the band that just before this period I'm talking about had musicians in it like Trummy Young -- I guess he sort of had his apprenticeship in Tommy Miles' band. It also had a tenor saxophone player and arranger whose name was Jimmy Mundy. There was also another trombone player whose name was Tyree Glenn. Tommy Miles probably had the best band in Washington, but these particular fellows, two years previous to the time I'm talking about, had gone to join Earl Hines' band, which was then featured at the Grand Terrace in Chicago.
And down the street there was a place called the Casino. A fellow named Booker Coleman had that band. And I never will forget... They had a sound something like Jimmy Lunceford.
